summary: Specifies a procedure using an OSPF LSA options bit to prevent routing loops in BGP/MPLS IP VPNs when the customer uses OSPFv2 with the provider. Without it, routes the provider sent to the customer might be sent back into the provider network. It is standards-track.

plainLanguage.summary: A route could travel in a circle: out to a customer and back. A tiny flag on the route says I came from the provider, so it is not sent around again.

subtitle: A single spare bit in OSPF link state advertisements stops VPN routes from looping back into BGP.

tldr.problem: In a BGP/MPLS IP VPN where a customer runs OSPFv2 with the provider, a route sent from a Provider Edge router to a customer can come back to another Provider Edge router with no sign that it came from the backbone, and could be pushed into BGP again.
tldr.mechanism: The high-order bit of the LSA Options field, called the DN bit, MUST be set on type 3, 5 and 7 LSAs sent from a PE to a CE, and a PE MUST NOT use such an LSA, when received from a CE, in its OSPF route calculation.
tldr.outcome: Routes learned through BGP are not redistributed back into BGP, which prevents routing loops. The bit has no other effect on how LSAs are stored or flooded.

sections.title: BGP/MPLS VPNs with OSPF at the Edge
sections.content:
In a BGP/MPLS IP VPN (RFC 4364), a service provider uses its IP backbone to give customers a private network service. A customer's edge devices (CE) connect to the provider's edge routers (PE). The CE and PE exchange routes using a routing protocol the customer and provider agree on.

The PE redistributes the routes it learns into BGP, using the VPN-IPv4 address family so that routes from different VPNs stay distinct even if they use the same private address space. The other PE routers turn those BGP routes back into ordinary routes for their own CEs. This is a peer model: CEs peer with PEs, but CEs at different sites do not peer with each other.

This RFC deals with the case where OSPFv2 runs on the PE-CE link. The PE then runs a separate OSPFv2 instance for each attached VPN. Procedures for the redistribution are in RFC 4577.
sections.plainLanguage: A company has offices that talk through a phone company. Each office hands its messages to the phone company, which delivers them to the other offices.

sections.title: How Information Loss Causes Loops
sections.content:
Suppose PE1 learns a VPN-IPv4 prefix through BGP and generates a summary LSA or an AS-external LSA that reports it. That LSA goes to CE1, spreads through the OSPF area, reaches CE2, and CE2 hands it to PE2.

PE2 must work out whether the prefix is reachable from CE2 by a path that includes no PE router. The RFC points out that there is no standard way to do this, because OSPFv2 LSAs do not necessarily carry the information needed to see that the path goes through PE1. If PE2 then leaks the prefix into BGP, it breaks a loop-freedom rule of BGP: routes learned from a BGP domain are not redistributed back into that domain. That could create a routing loop.

For AS-external LSAs, a PE could use a distinct tag value. That does not work for summary LSAs, and because each PE acts as an OSPF area 0 router, a summary LSA that originated at another PE can arrive over an area 0 PE-CE link. So a marking that works on every LSA type is needed.
sections.plainLanguage: A letter goes from the post office to a house and gets mailed right back to the post office, which does not realise it wrote the letter. Without a marker, the post office might send it out again and again.

sections.title: The DN Bit
sections.content:
The fix uses the high-order bit of the LSA Options field, a bit that was previously unused. The RFC calls it the DN bit. The Options field layout in RFC 2328 is shown as DN, a reserved bit, DC, EA, N/P, MC, E and another reserved bit.

  • When a type 3, 5 or 7 LSA is sent from a PE to a CE, the DN bit MUST be set.
  • The DN bit MUST be clear in all other LSA types.
  • When a PE receives a type 3, 5 or 7 LSA from a CE with the DN bit set, the information in that LSA MUST NOT be used in the OSPF route calculation. It is therefore not translated into a BGP route.
  • The DN bit MUST be ignored in all other LSA types.
sections.plainLanguage: Every note the phone company sends out gets a small stamp. If a note with that stamp ever comes back, the phone company throws it away instead of re-sending it.

sections.title: Effect on LSA Handling
sections.content:
The RFC says this restriction prevents routes learned via BGP from being redistributed to BGP. It compares this to the usual OSPF restriction that inter-area routes learned from area 0 are not passed back to area 0.

The DN bit has no other effect. An LSA with the DN bit set is put in the topological database, aged and flooded just as if the bit were not set. Only the PE's route calculation treats it differently.
sections.plainLanguage: The stamp only matters to the phone company. Everyone else handles the note exactly as before.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
An attacker could cause the DN bit to be set in an LSA travelling from CE to PE when it should be clear. The prefixes in that LSA could then become unreachable from other sites of the VPN.

An attacker could also cause the DN bit to be clear, in either direction, when it should be set. That could cause routing loops for traffic destined to the prefixes in the LSA.

The RFC says these possibilities can be eliminated by using cryptographic authentication as specified in Section D of the OSPFv2 specification.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone sneaks a stamp onto a note, or rubs it off, the note could get lost or go around in circles. A secret signature on each note stops that.
